news.title: Outside auditors find holes in OpenAI's internal agent monitor
news.summary: METR and Redwood Research spent three weeks inside OpenAI probing the system that watches its internal coding agents for misbehaviour. They found several weaknesses, including one that could have let an agent hide hundreds of actions; OpenAI says it has patched some of them.

news.title: OpenAI nears a $30B round at a lower $1.25T valuation
news.summary: OpenAI is close to a bridge round of up to $30 billion led by UAE investors and Coatue ahead of a possible IPO. The pre-money valuation of about $1.25 trillion is below the $1.4 trillion it had pitched earlier.

news.title: AWS capacity is sold out through 2027, Jassy says
news.summary: Amazon CEO Andy Jassy said nearly all of AWS's cloud capacity for 2026 and most of 2027 is already committed, with chunks of 2028 gone too. He put Amazon's 2026 capital spending at about $220 billion.

news.title: UK funds a £100M AI biosecurity lab backed by frontier labs
news.summary: The UK government will fund an independent non-profit lab to study how AI could be misused for biological threats. OpenAI and Anthropic have pledged compute and model access to the effort, part of a wider £600M package.

news.title: Google will use Gmail and Photos data for ads if Personal Intelligence is on
news.summary: A privacy-policy update lets Google personalize ads using Gmail and Photos content for users who opt in to its connected AI features. Users who leave Personal Intelligence off are not affected.

news.title: Canva launches its first in-house image-generation model
news.summary: Canva is rolling out its own image model to all users inside its design editor. It pitches the model as cheaper and easier to customize than third-party generators it relied on before.

news.title: Meta buys AI analytics startup Sundial
news.summary: Meta acquired Sundial, an AI data-analytics startup founded by former Meta executives including Julie Zhuo. The team joins a new Meta data-analytics group; terms were not disclosed.

news.title: Cambricon's profit jumps 148% as Chinese labs move off Nvidia
news.summary: Chinese AI chipmaker Cambricon reported third-quarter profit up 148% to about $210 million as domestic labs shift training work to its chips. Revenue still missed analyst forecasts.

news.title: PC shipments fall 21% as AI demand squeezes memory supply
news.summary: Counterpoint data show global PC shipments fell 21% year over year in Q3 2026. Rising memory and component prices, driven by AI data-center demand, are blamed, and a further drop is expected in Q4.

news.title: Agility Robotics standardizes Digit 5 humanoid on Nvidia IGX Thor
news.summary: Agility will use Nvidia's IGX Thor as the sole onboard computer for its next Digit humanoid. The company also said it has more than $300 million in multi-year orders.

news.title: Swedish government offices block ChatGPT and Claude
news.summary: Sweden's Government Offices will block ChatGPT and Claude on staff computers and direct employees to Microsoft Copilot instead. The move was announced on October 23.

news.title: US banks scramble to contain third-party AI agents in customer accounts
news.summary: Banks including Morgan Stanley and Bank of America are working out how to handle unvetted AI agents that customers let into their accounts. The hard question is telling whether an agent's action matches what the customer actually asked for.

papers.title: Harness²: Recursive Agent Harnessing for an Open World
papers.tldr: Harness² lets an AI agent improve its own instructions, tools and memory by comparing tweaked versions side by side, raising scores on professional-work benchmarks by up to about 12 points without retraining the model.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
Harness² lets an AI agent rewrite its own working setup (its instructions, tools and helper files) while it does a task, then carry the lessons it learned into future tasks, all without retraining the underlying model.

## Background you need
An LLM agent is a large language model that does multi-step work, such as running tools, writing files and checking results. The "harness" is everything wrapped around the model: the system prompt, safety rules, memory, reusable skills, tool tips, scripts and helper sub-agents. Recursive self-improvement means a system repeatedly edits its own setup to get better.

## The problem
Most attempts at self-improving agents assume there is an answer key. In coding, unit tests show whether an edit helped. Professional work, like drafting a report, has no automatic grader while the agent works. So the agent cannot tell if a harness change helped or hurt. Existing methods also tend to be tuned to one task type, so their improvements do not carry over to new kinds of work.

## The idea
Harness² swaps "is this correct?" for "is this version better than the last?" Think of a cook trying two tweaks to a recipe. They taste each version against the original and keep only clear improvements. Over time, they jot general lessons in a notebook for future recipes.

## How it works
1. **Treat the harness as editable files.** The harness is split into eight parts: system prompt, guardrails, memory, skills, tool guidance, scripts, sub-agents and a plug-in layer. The model's weights (its learned internal numbers) never change.
2. **Propose.** The agent first does the task once with its current harness, as a reference run. It then drafts two candidate edits. One targets general agent weaknesses, such as planning or tool use. The other targets knowledge and rules specific to the current field.
3. **Probe.** Each candidate is run on the same task under matched conditions. Its step-by-step trace and final output are compared with the reference run.
4. **Compose.** Only edits backed by that evidence are merged into the harness. The loop can repeat in parallel or in sequence; with several results, an AI judge compares anonymized outputs and picks the winner.
5. **Learn across tasks.** After each task, the system reviews its full edit history. It stores only evidence-backed lessons in a library that guides future tasks.

## Results
The authors tested on three professional-work benchmarks: WorkBuddy-Bench, JobBench and LAB. They used two models, GLM-5 and Gemini 3.5 Flash, each running inside two existing agent harnesses, OpenCode and Codex. That makes four model-and-harness combinations, compared against their unmodified base harnesses.

- The largest reported gains were up to 11.5 points on WorkBuddy-Bench, 4.5 points on JobBench and 11.8 percentage points on LAB.
- A single improvement round generally raised WorkBuddy-Bench scores. GLM-5 gained more in absolute terms than Gemini 3.5 Flash.
- Spending more effort on the per-task loop helped further. Parallel attempts added gains on JobBench and on partial pass rates in LAB.
- Removing any single ingredient hurt results: the two scoped candidates, the lesson library, or the merge step. The scoped candidates mattered most on JobBench.

## Why it matters
Teams often cannot retrain their models, but they control the harness. Harness² offers a way to improve agents on open-ended work using only the model they already have. It also shows that comparisons can stand in for an answer key.

## Caveats
Gains were not uniform. In one setting (Gemini under Codex on LAB partial pass rate), a competing method did better. Results depend on which model and harness are used, and the OpenCode-versus-Codex gap narrows but does not close. Testing covers only three benchmarks, two models and two harnesses. Each improvement round also needs extra full task runs, which adds compute cost.

## Key terms
- **Harness:** the instructions, tools, memory and helper code wrapped around a model that shape how it works.
- **Verifier:** an automatic checker that says whether an answer is right.
- **Propose–Probe–Compose:** draft candidate edits, test them against a reference run, keep only the proven changes.
- **Recursion budget:** how many improvement attempts the system is allowed per task.

papers.title: The Other Half of the Memory Wall: Serving 35B MoEs from SSD with Trained Routing Prediction
papers.tldr: Edge0 runs a 35-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model on a 24 GB Mac at about 20 tokens per second using under 3 GiB of memory, by streaming experts from the SSD and predicting which ones the next layer will need one word ahead.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
Edge0 runs a 35-billion-parameter AI model on a 24 GB Mac by keeping most of it on the SSD and using a small trained predictor to load the right pieces just in time.

## Background you need
A model's "weights" are the billions of numbers it learned. A mixture-of-experts model (MoE) splits much of itself into small sub-networks called experts, and a "router" picks a few per word. It computes with only a slice per word, but normally the whole thing must sit in memory. Quantization (storing numbers with fewer bits, here 4) shrinks it, but only so far.

## The problem
The model studied, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, uses about 3 billion of its 35 billion parameters per word. Yet at 4 bits it still takes 19.5 GB, too much for most laptops. Leaving experts on the SSD seems obvious. But each layer only picks its experts after the previous layer finishes, so a simple design waits on the disk at every layer, for every word.

## The idea
Edge0 guesses the next layer's experts one word ahead. Disk reads then overlap with current work. Think of a kitchen assistant who fetches the next ingredients from the basement before the chef asks. The twist: Edge0 uses the predicted experts as the real choice, so nothing fetched is wasted and nothing arrives late.

## How it works
1. **Experts live on the SSD.** Expert weights are stored in 4-bit form and read in small pieces on demand. A cache keeps popular experts in memory.
2. **A small "prerouter" per layer.** Each layer gets a tiny network. It sees the layer's output and which experts were used for this word and the previous one. It predicts the next layer's experts for the next word, starting from a copy of the real router.
3. **Training in three phases.** First, prerouters imitate the real routers. Second, a LoRA (a small set of extra trainable weights) is trained on about 2 million examples with predicted routing switched on; without it, output became repetitive. Third, the model writes its own text and the uncompressed original grades it, on about 200,000 examples.
4. **Keep the add-on separate.** The 42 MB LoRA runs alongside the 4-bit weights. Folding it in and re-compressing erased most of its benefit.

## Results
On a Mac mini M4 Pro with 24 GB of memory, the 35B model generated 20.4 tokens (word pieces) per second while using only 2.9 GiB of active memory. A standard setup holding all weights in memory managed 3.9 tokens per second and used 18.2 GiB. A smaller 8B version reached 28.0 tokens per second with 1.5 GiB.

Quality dropped modestly. Across five benchmarks (math, coding, science, knowledge, instruction following), the 35B model averaged 79.2 versus 83.2 for the uncompressed original. The biggest loss was on the AIME math contest: 86.6 versus 92.7.

On a 16 GB MacBook M2, where the model cannot fit in memory, the prerouter raised speed 80 to 84% over loading experts on demand. With four experts per layer, speed rose from 3.5 to 6.4 tokens per second, and disk waiting per step fell from 244 ms to about 102 ms.

## Why it matters
Capable models become practical on ordinary laptops, with no cloud server, which helps privacy, offline use and cost. It also highlights a less-studied bottleneck: stored weight size, not just working memory. Code, checkpoints and adapters are open source.

## Caveats
It serves one request at a time; batching was not studied. The prerouter helps less with warm caches or fast storage, and prefetching uses extra memory. Hard math lost the most quality, 10 points for the 8B model on AIME. Only Apple's MLX framework is supported. Single speed runs varied by up to 40%.

## Key terms
- **Mixture-of-experts (MoE):** a model built from many sub-networks, with only a few used per word.
- **Router:** the part of each layer that picks which experts to use.
- **Prerouter:** Edge0's small predictor that picks the next layer's experts one word early.
- **Quantization:** storing the model's numbers with fewer bits to save space.
- **LoRA:** a small set of extra trainable weights added to a frozen model to adjust its behavior.

papers.title: Prism: Dynamic Sparse Attention for Native 2K Joint Video-Audio Generation Model Training
papers.tldr: Prism trains a model that generates video and matching audio at 2K resolution about 2.5x faster than standard attention, by focusing compute on fast-changing and sound-producing regions.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
Prism trains an AI model that makes video and matching sound together at full 2K resolution. It runs about 2.5 times faster than the standard method because it skips the parts of the picture that matter little.

## Background you need
Modern video generators are often diffusion transformers. These models start from noise and clean it up step by step into a clip. They split the video into small patches called tokens. "Attention" is the step where each token looks at other tokens to decide what it should become.

## The problem
In full attention, every token compares itself with every other token. Double the tokens and the work roughly quadruples. A 2K clip (2560 by 1440 pixels) has far more tokens than a 720p clip, so training directly at 2K is very expensive.

The authors say cost is not the only issue. At high resolution, much of the attention goes to redundant tokens, like near-identical patches of sky. That spreads the learning signal thin and can disturb what the model already learned. Earlier "sparse attention" methods skip comparisons to save time. But most target speed when generating, not training, and they ignore how sound and picture interact.

## The idea
Think of a mapmaker who draws a busy city center street by street but covers an empty desert with a few big squares. Prism treats attention the same way. It uses fine detail where the picture changes quickly or where sound comes from, and coarse detail elsewhere. The key observation is that sound and picture interact mostly around the source of the sound, such as a singer's mouth or a drum being hit.

## How it works
1. **Split into zones.** The tokens are grouped into small 3D chunks covering space and time, called macro-zones. The released settings use chunks 4 tokens wide in each direction.
2. **Measure each zone.** Prism reads two cheap signals per zone. One is how much the video features vary, which shows how fast and in which direction the content changes. The other is how strongly the audio affects that region.
3. **Shape the blocks.** Attention works on blocks of tokens, not single tokens. Prism makes blocks thinner along directions of fast change or strong sound-picture coupling, so each block holds tokens that belong together.
4. **Keep only useful blocks.** Each group of tokens keeps a few top blocks, plus enough extra to cover most of the relevance. The released configs drop 75% to 93% of block pairs.
5. **Train at high resolution.** Prism starts from a pretrained video-audio model called MOVA. It then trains directly at 720p, 1080p and 2K with this sparse attention.

## Results
The authors report about a 2.5x training speedup over full attention. A run that took 10 days with full attention would take about 4. They also claim better output quality than full attention, not just equal quality. The paper body was not reachable for this summary, so specific quality scores and other baselines are not listed here.

Two preview models are public. Both turn an image and a text prompt into video with sound, at up to 2K.

## Why it matters
Attention cost has kept native 2K training out of reach for many open video projects. A 2.5x cut makes high-resolution video-audio models more practical to train and fine-tune. The code, training scripts and weights are open under the MIT license.

## Caveats
- Hardware needs remain high: at least 32 GPUs with 80 GB memory for 720p training, and 64 for 1080p or 2K.
- Generating at 1080p or 2K needs four or more such GPUs. 720p fits on one.
- The released models are previews; a stronger "pro" version is promised but not out.
- Public material gives few quality numbers, so independent checks of the quality claim matter.
- The method reads signals from the base model's audio-to-video layer, so it assumes such a layer exists.

## Key terms
- **Token:** a small patch of video or slice of audio handled as one unit.
- **Attention:** the step where tokens check each other to decide what to become.
- **Sparse attention:** attention that skips most token pairs to save compute.
- **Native 2K training:** training directly on 2K clips instead of upscaling smaller output.

papers.title: AI as a Compiler: Compiling Triton kernels without the Triton compiler
papers.tldr: An LLM agent translates Triton GPU kernels directly into NVIDIA PTX code, matching or beating Triton's own compiler on most kernels (up to 3.34× faster) under strict correctness checks.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
The authors let a large language model act as the compiler: it reads a GPU program written in Triton and writes the low-level machine-like code itself, often producing faster programs than Triton's own compiler.

## Background you need
GPUs run small, heavily optimized programs called kernels, which do jobs like matrix multiplication or attention. Triton is a popular Python-like language for writing kernels without deep hardware knowledge. Its compiler translates them, step by step, into PTX (NVIDIA's low-level assembly-like language for its GPUs). That translation is called "lowering".

## The problem
Easy kernel languages push the hard work into the compiler. Someone must hand-build many translation and optimization stages for every new hardware feature. Each new chip, like NVIDIA's Hopper or Blackwell, means more of this costly engineering. The compiler also only applies tricks its authors coded in.

## The idea
Skip the hand-built pipeline and let an AI model write the PTX directly. The authors call this "AI lowering". It is like a translator who rewrites a whole document fluently instead of following a fixed phrasebook. A strict testing harness then checks every output, so speed never comes at the cost of correctness.

## How it works
1. **A fixed setup.** An environment called TCEnv hands the model the Triton kernel plus fixed details: problem sizes, thread counts, target GPU, and a PTX template. The model only has to handle the translation.
2. **First draft.** An AI harness called TAIC, powered by a model named GPT-6 Astra, writes an initial PTX version. It can read profiler reports and look up PTX documentation.
3. **Test and measure.** TCEnv assembles the code, runs a memory-safety checker, compares outputs against the original Triton kernel on tricky random inputs, and times it.
4. **Plan and branch.** The model reads the results, names the main bottleneck, and writes an improvement plan. Helper agents try several independent patches.
5. **Keep only winners.** Only patches that compile, pass safety and correctness checks, and run faster seed the next round. This repeats until a dollar budget runs out. Optionally, an extended verifier called Volta can mathematically prove the PTX matches the original.

## Results
Baselines were autotuned Triton kernels (Triton automatically trying many settings). Tests ran on three NVIDIA GPUs: L40S, H100 and B200.

- Across 12 common kernels, AI lowering ran at 0.83× to 3.34× Triton's speed. Above 1× means faster.
- Simple kernels like ReLU landed within about 1% of Triton.
- Convolution reached up to 2.23×, by reusing data shared between overlapping windows.
- On ten kernels from recent research papers on B200, BitDelta hit 3.34×. The model decoded packed binary weights straight into Tensor Core inputs (Tensor Cores are the GPU's matrix-math units). FlashAttention reached 1.37×, by giving each thread a whole softmax row so threads need not share partial results.
- The weak spot: FP16 matrix multiplication on H100 ran at only 0.83×.
- Over five repeat runs, convolution averaged 2.00× and FlashAttention 1.24×.
- Costs per candidate kernel were usually under $1.50 for simple kernels and about $5 to $12 for convolution and matrix multiplication.
- Older models did worse on FP16 matrix multiplication: GPT-5.4 reached 0.73×, versus 1.00× for GPT-6 Astra.

## Why it matters
Bringing software to a new chip could need far less hand-written compiler work, which helps custom-accelerator makers most. AI also finds tricks fixed compiler rules never try.

## Caveats
Proof of correctness is costly in speed. Restricting to provably verified kernels dropped matrix multiplication from 1.03× to 0.24×. The verifier cannot handle atomic operations, data-dependent branching, or bit-level tricks. Only the newest model gave competitive results. Generation costs dollars and time, versus milliseconds for Triton. Most experiments ran once, and the work covers only Triton to PTX on NVIDIA GPUs at fixed problem sizes.

## Key terms
- **Kernel**: a small program that runs one operation on the GPU.
- **Triton**: a Python-like language for writing GPU kernels more easily.
- **PTX**: NVIDIA's low-level, assembly-like code for its GPUs.
- **Lowering**: translating high-level code into lower-level code the hardware can run.
- **Formal verification**: mathematically proving two programs always produce the same result.

papers.title: Post-hoc Epistemic Uncertainty for Vision-Language-Action Policies
papers.tldr: A cheap add-on that compares a robot policy's internal state to its training demonstrations tells the robot when it is out of its depth about as well as running two policies, at up to 50 times lower scoring cost.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
The authors bolt a small, cheap add-on onto a finished robot policy so it can tell when it is facing a situation it was never trained on, without retraining the robot's brain or running a second copy of it.

## Background you need
A vision-language-action policy (a model that looks at camera images, reads an instruction like "put the mug in the basket", and outputs arm movements) is the current favourite way to control robot arms. "Epistemic uncertainty" means uncertainty that comes from missing knowledge: the robot simply has not seen enough examples like this one. That kind of uncertainty can be fixed by collecting more demonstrations, unlike pure randomness in the world.

## The problem
A robot that does not know what it does not know will confidently fail. Ideally it should say "I'm unsure here" so a person can step in or record a new demonstration.

Today's best signal comes from an ensemble: train two or more policies and measure how much they disagree. That works, but it doubles the cost of pre-training, fine-tuning and running the robot. Cheaper single-model signals, such as how "surprised" the language part of the model is, turn out to be almost useless in the authors' tests.

## The idea
Think of a tour guide with a notebook of every street they have walked. When a tourist asks about a place, the guide checks how close it is to anything in the notebook. Far from every entry means "I'm guessing here".

The paper does the same with the policy's internal summaries (embeddings, the lists of numbers a model computes to describe what it sees). It stores the embeddings of all training demonstrations. At run time it measures how far the current situation sits from that stored collection.

## How it works
1. **Freeze the policy.** The robot model (SmolVLA, a compact open policy) is left untouched. Nothing is retrained and no labels are needed.
2. **Collect embeddings.** For every frame in the training demonstrations, the method records an internal summary. One version reads the summary of cameras, instruction and robot state. Another reads the hidden state of the part that generates actions.
3. **Tidy the space.** The numbers are rescaled and compressed to a few hundred directions, so no single feature dominates the distance.
4. **Score with a Gaussian process.** A Gaussian process (a classic statistical tool that knows how confident it is between known data points) gives a variance score. It is near 1 far from the demonstrations and near 0 close to them.
5. **Use the score.** The number can rank tasks by likely failure, choose which new demonstrations to collect, or decide when to hand control to a stronger "supervisor" policy.

## Results
Tests use LIBERO-10, a simulated benchmark of ten long kitchen-and-household manipulation tasks.

- **Predicting failure across tasks.** The cameras-and-instruction head reached a correlation of 0.77 (rank) and 0.82 (linear) with task failure. The previous best ensemble signal scored 0.75 and 0.64. The language model's own confidence scored around zero, meaning it carried no useful information.
- **Early on, it helps most.** Before any extra data was collected, the new head reached 0.94 linear correlation versus 0.75 for the ensemble.
- **Much cheaper.** Setting it up was about 44 times faster per fine-tuning round, and scoring was up to about 50 times faster than ensemble methods. In practice, one policy does the job of two.
- In choosing demonstrations to collect and deciding when to defer, the authors report the heads are competitive with the ensemble.

The authors also found a flaw in the benchmark itself. A trivial score that just counts demonstrations per task reached 0.82 rank correlation. So the standard test mostly rewards knowing which tasks had less data. They added 20 families of controlled changes (moved cameras, reworded instructions, shifted objects) to test harder cases.

## Why it matters
Robots that know when to ask for help are safer and cheaper to teach. This method lets teams add that ability to an existing open policy in minutes, not a second training run. It also gives a practical tool for deciding which demonstrations are worth recording next, which is the main cost in robot learning.

## Caveats
Only one policy (SmolVLA) and one simulated benchmark were tested, with three random seeds. No real-robot results are reported. The method cannot cleanly separate "missing knowledge" from inherent ambiguity. Its quality depends on the policy's embeddings keeping unfamiliar situations apart, which training does not guarantee. The exact Gaussian process is fine at this scale but may need approximations for very large datasets.

## Key terms
- **Vision-language-action policy:** a model mapping camera images plus a text instruction to robot motions.
- **Epistemic uncertainty:** doubt caused by lack of training data, fixable with more examples.
- **Ensemble disagreement:** running several models and treating their disagreement as a sign of doubt.
- **Embedding:** a list of numbers a model uses internally to summarize its input.
- **Gaussian process:** a statistical method that estimates both a value and how unsure it is, based on distance to known data.
- **LIBERO-10:** a simulated benchmark of ten long, multi-step manipulation tasks.

papers.title: WeVisOne-VL: Unified Visual Perception from Objects to Pixels
papers.tldr: Tencent's WeVisOne-VL is a small open vision-language model that detects, counts, points at, reads, segments and cuts out objects from text prompts in one system, and reliably says when an object is not there.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
Tencent's WeChat Vision team built one small open model that can find, count, point at, read, outline and precisely cut out things in an image, all from a plain-text request.

## Background you need
A vision-language model (VLM) is an AI that looks at an image and answers in text, like a chatbot with eyes. "Perception" tasks ask it *where* things are, not just *what* they are. Answers range from coarse to fine: a point, a bounding box (a rectangle around an object), a segmentation mask (the exact pixels of the object), or an alpha matte (a mask with soft, partly transparent edges, like hair or glass).

## The problem
Chat-style VLMs describe images well but localize unreliably. Ask for every apple in a crowded crate and they miss many. Ask about something absent and they often invent a box. For pixel-level work, builders bolt on separate segmentation or matting tools, adding models, failure points and engineering.

## The idea
Treat every perception task as the model "writing" a structured answer, one token (word-piece) at a time. Boxes become special number tokens. For fine detail, a marker token hands off to a tiny pixel specialist. Think of a site manager who notes "the blue crate, top left" and calls a craftsman to trace its exact outline.

## How it works
1. **Start from a strong base.** It builds on Qwen3-VL, an open VLM, in 2B and 4B sizes (billions of parameters).
2. **Speak in coordinates.** Positions use dedicated tokens `<0>` to `<1000>` on a normalized grid. If the object is absent, the model answers "None" instead of guessing.
3. **Hand off to a pixel decoder.** After each predicted box, the model writes an `<OBJ>` token. A 9.6-million-parameter decoder reads that token's internal state, the box, and multi-layer image features. It refines a full-resolution mask or matte, coarse to fine.
4. **Build labeled data.** A data engine guided by a knowledge graph (a map of related concepts) finds object types, localizes them with expert models, verifies them with a VLM, and extends boxes to masks and mattes. Over 100 million images were labeled this way.
5. **Train in stages.** Three supervised fine-tuning stages (learning from labeled examples) run as a curriculum. A final reinforcement learning stage (learning from scored attempts) mixes all tasks.

## Results
The authors report leading results on over 30 benchmarks, against general VLMs (Qwen3-VL-8B, Qwen3.5-9B) and specialists (Rex-Omni-3B, LocateAnything-3B). F1 blends precision and recall; higher is better.
- **Crowded scenes:** on Dense200 detection, the 4B model scores 71.3 versus 58.7 for the best rival.
- **Saying "not here":** on their WeRef-Bench, it correctly refuses 96.4% of queries about absent objects, versus 73.0% for the best baseline.
- **Counting:** 89.6% exact-match accuracy on PixMo-Count, versus 82.8%.
- **Text in images:** 52.0 F1 on TotalText (curved scene text), versus 43.3.
- **Reasoning segmentation:** 71.2 on ReasonSeg, versus 65.0 for LISA-13B, a model several times larger.
- **Matting:** average pixel error on P3M-500-NP falls from 15.4 (SAM-based matting) to 7.3, roughly halving edge mistakes.

## Why it matters
One compact model can replace a stack of detectors, segmenters and matting tools. That simplifies background removal, visual search or receipt reading. A reliable "None" answer makes automation safer. Open weights let researchers build on it.

## Caveats
- The 4B model does not win everything; the 2B version beats it on some matting tests.
- Some headline numbers use the authors' own new benchmarks (WeRef-Bench, WeRefMat).
- Soft edges degrade with low resolution, heavy occlusion or complex transparency, and depend on prompt wording.
- Single images only; no video, and no step-by-step reasoning.
- This summary draws on the abstract, model cards and code repository; the arXiv full text could not be fetched.

## Key terms
- **Bounding box:** a rectangle drawn tightly around an object.
- **Segmentation mask:** a pixel-exact cutout marking which pixels belong to an object.
- **Alpha matte:** a cutout with soft, partly transparent edges for hair, fur or glass.
- **Referring localization:** finding the object a phrase describes, like "the man in the red hat".
- **Rejection rate:** how often the model correctly says an asked-for object is not in the image.
